{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that the intervention training (based on the 4C/ID model and focused on situational awareness, tactical gaze control, and visual attention) would improve the time until the first hit in shoot scenarios to a greater extent than the active control training.",
  "design": "mixed, 2 (group: intervention vs. control) x 2 (measurement time: pre-test vs. post-test)",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "An individual video-based intervention training grounded on the Four-Component Instructional Design Model (4C/ID) versus an active control training resembling traditional police firearms training.",
  "outcome_measure": "Time (in milliseconds) between the detection of the black handgun and the first effective hit in predefined areas (torso or head) during realistic shoot/don't shoot video scenarios.",
  "population_and_setting": "N = 45 senior police officers recruited from the German Police University, tested in an indoor firing range lab setting.",
  "sample_size_total": 45,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Recruited via notices on campus; participation was voluntary; debriefed at the end of the study.",
  "analysis_plan": "Repeated measures ANOVA with the within-subject factor Time and the between-subject factor Group.",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "preregistered (www.aspredicted.org #119896)",
  "other_methods_notes": "Participants used a gas-operated replica of a Heckler and Koch SFP9 handgun. Eye-tracking glasses were worn during tests. The intervention training included educational videos and practical exercises focused on situational awareness, tactical gaze control, and visual attention. The control training focused on speed-accuracy trade-offs in marksmanship."
}
